To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) people overestimate their performances on difficult tasks and underestimate their performances on easy tasks; (b) on difficult tasks, people mistakenly believe that they perform worse than others, but on easy tasks, they mistakenly believe that they outperform others; (c) overestimation is greater than underestimation, but underestimation is greater on easy tasks; and (d) people are overprecise, but overprecision reduces the magnitude of overestimation and of overplacement.

(a) people overestimate their own performance and overplace their performance relative to others on difficult tasks but underestimate their own performance and underplace their performance relative on easy tasks and (b) overprecision reduces the magnitude of overestimation and of overplacement.

(a) overplacement is a stronger predictor of overconfidence than overestimation, (b) people tend to be overconfident about difficult tasks but underconfident about easy tasks, and (c), when they are overconfident, they are overprecise.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of overconfidence.
the question of whether people are too confident, and if so, how this affects their performance and decision making.
the relationship between overconfidence and performance and the conditions under which overconfidence is beneficial or harmful. (Contains 2 figures and 2 tables.)
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
overconfidence is not a single, unitary phenomenon but a complex set of phenomena that are related in important ways.
overconfidence is a pervasive phenomenon, but it is also a complex and multifaceted one.
overprecision is the most pervasive and most harmful form of overconfidence, and it is a distinct phenomenon that can be distinguished from overestimation and from overplacement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people are often too sure of their beliefs and that this overprecision is a pervasive and pernicious form of overconfidence.
overconfidence is not a unitary construct but rather an umbrella term for a variety of distinct phenomena.
people overconfidently believe their beliefs are more accurate than they really are. (Contains 1 table and 1 figure.)
The main takeaway from our work is that
the various types of overconfidence are not interchangeable and that the presence of 1 type does not imply the presence of the other types.
